question: Two hotels report the same RevPAR. Does that mean they're performing equally well? Why or why not?
lookingFor: Understanding that RevPAR combines occupancy and rate, and that the same number can hide very different underlying strategies.

bullets: Define RevPAR as occupancy multiplied by average daily rate
Explain that identical RevPAR can come from a high-occupancy, low-rate hotel or a low-occupancy, high-rate hotel
Note that the two strategies carry different cost structures and guest experiences, so the same number isn't the same performance
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: RevPAR is occupancy times average daily rate, so a hotel running at ninety percent occupancy on a low rate can land on exactly the same RevPAR as one running fifty percent occupancy on a much higher rate. Those are really different businesses, the first is spending more on housekeeping, staffing, and wear on the building to serve far more guests, while the second has lower variable costs but is more exposed if demand softens. I'd want to look at GOPPAR or cost per occupied room alongside RevPAR before saying either one is doing better. It's the kind of metric that's useful for tracking trends but dangerous to compare in isolation.

commonMistakes: Treating RevPAR as a complete measure of profitability
Being unable to state the formula correctly
Not recognizing that occupancy and rate can trade off against each other
followUps: What other metric would you want to see alongside RevPAR to judge performance properly?

question: Several cities have introduced strict limits on short-term rental platforms like Airbnb. What's your view on this kind of regulation?
lookingFor: Balanced awareness of the housing and community arguments against the tourism and hospitality diversification arguments, with a reasoned personal position.

bullets: Name the core tension, housing availability and neighborhood character versus tourism flexibility and local income
Show awareness that hotels and short-term rentals compete on an uneven regulatory playing field
Land on a considered position rather than a flat pro or anti stance
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Cities like Barcelona and New York have tightened rules because short-term rentals were pulling long-term housing out of the market and pushing up rents for residents, which is a real cost that tourism revenue doesn't fully offset. At the same time, I understand the frustration from hotels, they operate under licensing, tax, and safety rules that a lot of short-term rental hosts simply don't, so the competition wasn't ever fair to begin with. My honest view is that some regulation makes sense, but it needs to distinguish between someone renting a spare room occasionally and a company running dozens of units as a shadow hotel business. I think the smartest policy targets the second group without punishing the first.

commonMistakes: Taking a purely pro-tourism or purely pro-regulation stance with no nuance
Not knowing any real examples of cities that have acted on this
Ignoring the competitive fairness angle between hotels and platforms
followUps: How do you think this affects a hotel's pricing strategy in a city that tightens these rules?

question: Sites like Auschwitz or Chernobyl draw large numbers of tourists every year. Is it ethical to build a tourism industry around places of tragedy?
lookingFor: Nuanced ethical reasoning distinguishing respectful remembrance from exploitation, rather than a blanket approval or rejection.

bullets: Acknowledge the genuine tension between education or remembrance and profiting from suffering
Distinguish between how a site is managed, memorial-led versus spectacle-led, as the real ethical hinge
Reach a considered position that doesn't dismiss the whole category as inherently wrong or automatically fine
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think the existence of tourism at a site like Auschwitz is unethical in itself, if anything, visiting and understanding what happened there is part of how a tragedy stays remembered rather than forgotten. What I'd push back on is when a site gets treated as a spectacle, souvenir stalls, selfie culture, or tour operators racing groups through without context, because that's when remembrance slides into exploitation. I think the ethics really sit in how it's managed, whether the revenue and experience are designed around education and dignity or around volume and entertainment. As a manager, I'd want to see local communities and survivor organizations genuinely involved in shaping how the site is presented, not just consulted after the fact.

commonMistakes: Declaring all dark tourism either fully acceptable or fully wrong with no reasoning
Ignoring the management and presentation angle entirely
Showing no awareness of a real example
followUps: Who do you think should have the final say over how a site like that is presented to tourists?

question: Elephant riding and similar animal encounters remain popular tourist attractions in some destinations despite animal welfare concerns. If you managed a tour operator offering this, what would you do?
lookingFor: Willingness to prioritize welfare over short-term revenue, with realistic thinking about how to transition a business rather than simply moralizing.

bullets: State a clear ethical position on the welfare concerns rather than staying neutral
Recognize the practical difficulty, revenue, local livelihoods, and animal sanctuaries all depend on some funding stream
Propose a realistic path, such as shifting toward observation-based or sanctuary-model experiences instead of an abrupt shutdown
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I wouldn't want to keep offering elephant riding once I understood the training methods and physical strain typically involved, the welfare evidence on that is fairly well established at this point. But I also know that abruptly pulling the product could hurt the mahouts and local workers who depend on that income, so I wouldn't just cancel it overnight without a plan. I'd look at what some operators have already done, transitioning toward observation and bathing experiences at ethical sanctuaries, and I'd use my existing customer base and marketing to build demand for that alternative before fully switching over. It's a business decision as much as an ethical one, and I think the two can align if you manage the transition properly instead of treating it as pure loss.

commonMistakes: Refusing to take a clear position on the welfare issue
Ignoring the economic impact on local workers entirely
Proposing an unrealistic instant shutdown with no transition plan
followUps: How would you handle customers who specifically ask for the riding experience you've phased out?

question: Hotels increasingly use guest data and AI to personalize service, remembering preferences, predicting needs, even adjusting pricing. Where do you think the line should be drawn on privacy?
lookingFor: Balanced reasoning about the genuine service benefits of data use against real privacy risk, with a specific line rather than a vague concern.

bullets: Acknowledge the real service benefit, personalization can make a guest feel genuinely well cared for
Identify a specific privacy risk, such as data being used without clear consent or shared beyond the property
Propose a concrete boundary, like transparency and opt-in rather than silent data collection
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I like the idea of a hotel remembering I prefer a firm pillow or always order the same breakfast, that kind of personalization is what makes a stay feel considered rather than generic. Where it gets uncomfortable is if that data gets used in ways guests never agreed to, like adjusting prices based on browsing behavior or sharing preferences with third parties without saying so. My line would be transparency, tell guests clearly what's being collected and let them opt in, rather than quietly building a profile behind the scenes. I think guests are usually fine trading some data for better service, but only when they know the trade is happening.

commonMistakes: Treating all data use as either entirely fine or entirely creepy
No concrete example of where personalization helps or where it goes wrong
Not proposing any actual boundary or principle
followUps: Would your answer change if the guest never explicitly consented but the data made their stay noticeably better?

question: A major storm has just been announced and is forcing mass evacuations. Room demand near the evacuation zone spikes overnight. As the hotel's revenue manager, would you raise your rates?
lookingFor: Recognition that standard yield management logic breaks down ethically in an emergency, with a defensible alternative approach.

bullets: Distinguish normal demand-based pricing from price gouging in a genuine emergency
Consider the legal and reputational risk alongside the ethical one, many places have anti-gouging laws in disasters
Propose a concrete alternative, holding or capping rates and using the moment to build long-term trust
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: No, I wouldn't raise rates in that situation, even though the textbook yield management logic says demand spikes justify higher prices. This isn't normal discretionary demand, it's people who need shelter urgently, and a lot of jurisdictions actually have anti-price-gouging laws that kick in during declared emergencies, so it could be illegal as well as unethical. I'd hold rates steady or even offer an evacuation rate, and I think that decision pays off longer term too, guests remember which hotels treated them fairly under pressure, and that kind of goodwill is worth more than one inflated night's revenue. Revenue management is a tool for normal market conditions, not a rule that overrides basic decency in a crisis.

commonMistakes: Defending the price increase purely on supply-and-demand logic with no ethical consideration
Not knowing that gouging laws often apply during declared emergencies
Failing to connect the decision to longer-term brand reputation
followUps: What would you say to an owner who pushed back and wanted you to maximize revenue regardless?

question: What do you understand by the term 'ghost kitchen', and what do you think it means for the future of restaurants?
lookingFor: Accurate grasp of the delivery-only kitchen model and a reasoned view of its impact on the traditional restaurant experience.

bullets: Define a ghost kitchen as a delivery-only kitchen with no dining room, often serving multiple brands from one space
Explain the business logic, lower rent and staffing costs, built around delivery app demand
Offer a view on what it might mean for dine-in hospitality and guest experience
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A ghost kitchen is a kitchen built purely to fulfill delivery orders, often through apps like Uber Eats or DoorDash, with no dining room, and sometimes one kitchen runs several different virtual brands out of the same space to spread costs. The appeal is obvious financially, you skip the rent, front-of-house staff, and design costs of a full restaurant while still reaching customers. My honest view is that it's a smart economic model but it strips away most of what I'd call hospitality, there's no service moment, no atmosphere, just food arriving at a door. I think it'll keep growing alongside traditional restaurants rather than replacing them, because people will always want some occasions to actually go out and be looked after.

commonMistakes: Confusing a ghost kitchen with a normal restaurant offering delivery as an extra channel
No mention of the cost structure that makes the model attractive
No opinion on what it means for the guest experience
followUps: Do you think ghost kitchens count as part of the hospitality industry, or are they something separate?

question: Some restaurants have tried removing tipping entirely and building service charges into menu prices instead. What do you think of that approach?
lookingFor: Awareness of the real trade-offs between tipped and no-tip models for staff income, guest expectations, and business viability.

bullets: Explain the case for removing tipping, more predictable pay, less pressure on servers to perform for tips, fairer pooling with kitchen staff
Explain the case against, some experienced servers earn less, and guests sometimes resist visibly higher menu prices
Give a considered personal view rather than declaring one model obviously correct
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The case for removing tipping is real, it gives servers predictable income instead of relying on unpredictable guest generosity, and it lets a restaurant actually share revenue fairly with kitchen staff, who never see tips under the traditional model despite doing just as much of the work. The problem I've read about is that some strong servers in busy, high-turnover restaurants were earning more under tips than the built-in service charge replaces, so it isn't a clean win for everyone on staff. I think the approach makes sense for restaurants trying to build a more equitable culture across the whole team, but it has to be paired with genuinely raising base pay, not just relabeling the same total cost. My honest view is it's the fairer system long term, even if the transition is uncomfortable for some staff and guests.

commonMistakes: Only presenting one side of the debate
Assuming removing tips automatically means better pay for everyone
No awareness that this is an active, real debate in the industry
followUps: How would you explain a built-in service charge to a guest used to tipping who feels annoyed by it?

question: Imagine you're appointed tourism manager for a small historic town that's just gone viral online and is now seeing ten times its usual visitor numbers. What would your first three moves be?
lookingFor: Structured, prioritized crisis thinking that balances resident wellbeing, infrastructure limits, and not simply rejecting the economic opportunity.

bullets: Prioritize immediate, practical steps, like managing crowd flow, sanitation, and resident access, over long-term branding
Show awareness that residents' quality of life has to be part of the plan, not an afterthought
Suggest a mechanism to capture and reinvest the tourism revenue rather than just absorbing the strain for free
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: First I'd focus on the immediate strain, working out where the physical bottlenecks are, narrow streets, parking, toilets, and putting quick fixes in place like timed entry to the busiest spots or extra sanitation, because that's what stops the sudden popularity turning into visible damage or resident anger fast. Second, I'd talk directly to residents and local businesses, because if this town becomes known as unlivable for locals, the backlash usually kills the tourism appeal within a couple of years anyway. Third, I'd look at introducing something like a small visitor contribution or parking fee that's clearly reinvested into the town's upkeep, so residents can see the tourism paying for the strain it causes rather than just tolerating it. I'd rather manage the surge deliberately than either shut it down entirely or let it run unmanaged.

commonMistakes: Jumping straight to banning or capping tourists with no other strategy
Ignoring resident wellbeing and focusing purely on visitor experience
A vague answer with no concrete first steps
followUps: What would you do if local business owners actively wanted the surge to continue unmanaged for the extra income?

question: Hotel loyalty programs give away free nights and upgrades. Why would a hotel chain willingly give up that revenue?
lookingFor: Understanding of loyalty programs as a customer acquisition and retention investment, not simply lost revenue.

bullets: Explain that loyalty rewards are funded by the value of repeat, direct bookings that bypass costly third-party commissions
Note the data and personalization value chains get from tracking loyal guest behavior over time
Recognize the trade-off, programs cost real money and only work if the retained value exceeds it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It looks like giving revenue away, but a loyalty program is really an investment in getting guests to book directly instead of through an online travel agent that charges the hotel a hefty commission, so a free night funded by points can still be cheaper than paying commission on several paid stays. It also builds a dataset the chain can use, knowing a guest's room preference or spending pattern lets them personalize offers and increase spend on things like food and spa over time. The trade-off is real though, if the rewards are too generous relative to what loyal guests actually spend, the program becomes a cost center rather than a growth engine, which is why chains constantly tweak the earn and redemption rates. It's less charity and more a calculated bet on lifetime guest value.

commonMistakes: Treating loyalty programs as pure marketing goodwill with no financial logic
Not mentioning online travel agent commissions as the comparison point
Assuming loyalty programs are always profitable with no downside
followUps: How might a hotel measure whether its loyalty program is actually worth the cost?

question: What are the trade-offs between owning an independent hotel and operating as a franchise of a major brand?
lookingFor: Clear grasp of the real costs and benefits on both sides, not a one-sided view of franchising as purely good or purely restrictive.

bullets: Explain the franchise benefit, brand recognition, loyalty program access, and centralized booking systems
Explain the franchise cost, ongoing fees and reduced creative or operational control
Explain the independent trade-off, full control and unique identity, but harder-won visibility and no built-in guest pipeline
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A franchise gets instant brand recognition and plugs straight into a loyalty program and a global booking system, which can be a huge advantage for filling rooms, especially somewhere without much natural footfall. The cost is real though, ongoing franchise fees eat into margins, and you often have to follow brand standards on everything from room layout to the type of soap you use, which limits how distinctive the property can be. An independent hotel keeps full creative and operational control, which suits a property trying to build a genuinely unique identity, but it has to build its own visibility and guest trust from scratch, without the built-in pipeline a big brand name provides. I think the right choice really depends on the location, a property in a competitive city with strong footfall can probably succeed independently, while one relying on business travelers who book through familiar systems probably benefits more from the franchise route.

commonMistakes: Only describing one side, franchise or independent, without a genuine trade-off
Not mentioning franchise fees or brand standard restrictions
No reasoning about when one model suits a property better than the other
followUps: Which model do you think you'd rather manage, and why?

question: Apps that let hospitality businesses book short-notice, gig-style staff for a single shift are becoming common. What do you think this means for the industry's workforce?
lookingFor: Balanced view of the flexibility benefits against job security and training concerns, grounded in real industry context.

bullets: Explain the appeal for businesses, filling last-minute gaps without the overhead of permanent hires
Explain the appeal and risk for workers, flexibility and choice of shifts versus no job security or benefits
Consider the effect on service quality and team consistency when staff rotate frequently
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: For a business, gig staffing apps are genuinely useful for covering a sudden sickness or an unexpectedly busy weekend without carrying extra permanent headcount all year, which matters given how seasonal a lot of hospitality demand is. For workers it cuts both ways, some people genuinely want that flexibility to pick up shifts around study or other jobs, but it also means no sick pay, no real job security, and none of the training investment that builds a strong long-term team. My concern from a service quality angle is that hospitality really depends on staff who know the property, the regular guests, and each other, and a rotating cast of one-off gig workers can't build that. I think it's a useful tool for genuine short-notice gaps, but a business relying on it as its core staffing model is probably trading away consistency it'll miss.

commonMistakes: Only seeing the flexibility benefit with no downside for workers
Not connecting the trend to service quality or team consistency
Treating this as a purely negative development with no acknowledgment of real business need
followUps: Would you rely on gig staffing for a role that deals directly with guests, or keep that in-house? Why?

subtopic: Food cost percentage and menu engineering
question: A dish costs a restaurant four dollars to make and sells for twenty. Another costs twelve dollars and sells for thirty. Which one would you rather push on the menu, and why?
lookingFor: Understanding that food cost percentage alone can mislead, and that gross profit per dish, alongside likely sales volume, matters more.

bullets: Calculate food cost percentage for both, twenty percent versus forty percent
Show that the higher-cost-percentage dish still generates more gross profit per plate, eighteen dollars versus sixteen
Note that the real decision also depends on likely sales volume and how each fits the menu's overall positioning
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: On food cost percentage alone the first dish looks much better, it's twenty percent food cost against forty percent for the second. But if I look at actual gross profit per plate, the first makes sixteen dollars and the second makes eighteen, so the higher percentage dish is actually more profitable per sale despite looking worse on that one ratio. I wouldn't decide purely on either number though, I'd also want to know which one guests are more likely to order and how it fits with the rest of the menu, a great margin on a dish nobody chooses doesn't help the bottom line. I think the mistake a lot of new managers make is chasing the lowest food cost percentage instead of the highest actual profit contribution.

commonMistakes: Choosing based on food cost percentage alone without calculating actual profit
Getting the arithmetic wrong
Ignoring the role of expected sales volume in the real decision
followUps: How might you use the menu's layout or descriptions to steer guests toward the more profitable dish?

question: You're the hospitality director on a cruise ship, and a norovirus outbreak has just been confirmed among passengers on day two of a seven-day voyage. What would you do?
lookingFor: Structured crisis response prioritizing containment and honest communication over minimizing the problem for commercial reasons.

bullets: Prioritize immediate containment, enhanced sanitation, isolating affected guests, restricting self-service food areas
Emphasize transparent communication with all passengers rather than downplaying the outbreak
Consider the harder call, whether to alter the itinerary or cut the voyage short, and weigh guest safety against commercial cost
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first priority would be containment, working with the medical team to isolate affected passengers, sharply increasing sanitation protocols, and probably switching self-service buffets to staff-served food immediately, since that's a known transmission point. I'd want honest, calm communication to all passengers about what's happening and what we're doing, because rumors spread faster than facts on a ship and vague reassurance usually backfires. The harder decision is whether to alter the itinerary, maybe skip a port to avoid spreading it ashore, or even cut the voyage short if containment isn't working, and I'd rather take that commercial hit than have the outbreak get worse or reach the local community we're visiting. Passenger and crew safety has to come before finishing the itinerary as planned.

commonMistakes: Minimizing the outbreak to protect the guest experience or commercial schedule
No concrete containment steps, only vague reassurance
Ignoring the possibility of altering the itinerary as an option
followUps: How would you handle passengers demanding refunds for a shortened voyage?

question: Critics argue that all-inclusive resorts in developing destinations capture most tourist spending while contributing little to the local economy. What's your take on that criticism?
lookingFor: Understanding of the concept of economic leakage in tourism, balanced against the real employment and infrastructure resorts do provide.

bullets: Explain economic leakage, money spent that flows back to foreign owners, imported goods, or head offices rather than staying local
Acknowledge the genuine local benefit, employment, training, and infrastructure that resorts do provide
Suggest a way this tension can be reduced rather than treating the model as simply good or bad
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: There's real substance to the criticism, when a resort is foreign owned, imports much of its food and supplies, and guests never leave the property to spend at local restaurants or shops, a lot of the tourist dollar leaks straight back out of the destination's economy instead of circulating locally. That said, I don't think it's fair to say resorts contribute nothing, they're often major employers and can bring infrastructure like roads or water systems that benefit the wider area too. I think the fix isn't rejecting the all-inclusive model outright, it's destinations negotiating harder on local sourcing requirements and encouraging resorts to build in optional excursions that actually get guests spending in the local community. It's a genuine trade-off, and I don't think either side of the debate has the full picture on its own.

commonMistakes: Not knowing the term or concept of economic leakage
Taking a one-sided view, either resorts are purely exploitative or purely beneficial
No suggestion of how the tension might actually be addressed
followUps: What could a resort itself do, without government intervention, to reduce this leakage?

question: It's become easier to generate large numbers of fake positive reviews, or even use AI tools to write them. As a hotel manager, would you ever consider using something like this to boost your ratings?
lookingFor: A firm ethical line against fabricated reviews, with reasoning about long-term trust and the real alternative of earning reviews honestly.

bullets: State clearly that fabricated reviews are dishonest to guests making decisions based on them
Note the practical risk too, platforms increasingly detect and penalize this, and it can seriously damage a business if exposed
Propose a legitimate alternative, actively prompting real satisfied guests to leave honest reviews
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: No, I wouldn't do that, and it's not just about getting caught, it's that reviews exist so guests can trust what previous visitors actually experienced, and faking that undermines the whole system everyone in the industry relies on. Practically, it's also a bad bet, review platforms are getting better at detecting suspicious patterns, and if a hotel gets flagged or exposed, the reputational damage is far worse than a few mediocre honest reviews would have been. What I'd do instead is make it genuinely easy for satisfied guests to leave a review, a friendly prompt at checkout or a follow-up email, because real reviews from real stays are both more trustworthy and more sustainable. I'd rather build a rating slowly and honestly than risk the business's credibility on something fabricated.

commonMistakes: Treating this as acceptable if it's unlikely to get caught
Focusing only on the risk of punishment rather than the underlying dishonesty
No alternative offered for genuinely improving ratings
followUps: What would you do if you discovered a competitor was doing this and it was working for them?

question: What do you understand by the term 'emotional labor', and why is it particularly relevant to hospitality work?
lookingFor: Accurate grasp of the concept as managing one's own displayed emotions as part of the job, with awareness of its cost to staff wellbeing.

bullets: Define emotional labor as the effort of managing and displaying particular emotions as part of a job, regardless of how you actually feel
Explain why hospitality demands this constantly, staying warm and patient with every guest interaction, including difficult ones
Connect it to staff burnout and the case for management supporting staff through it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Emotional labor is the work of managing your own emotions to present a particular face to the customer, staying warm, patient, and upbeat, even if you're exhausted or the guest in front of you is being unreasonable. It's especially relevant to hospitality because that performance is almost constant, a front desk agent might handle a dozen difficult check-ins in a row and still has to sound genuinely pleased to help on the next one. I think it's a real cost that's often invisible in how the job gets described, and it's a big part of why burnout is common in guest-facing roles. As a manager I'd want to actively build in recovery time and real support, not just tell staff to smile through it, because that emotional effort adds up over a shift in a way physical tasks alone don't.

commonMistakes: Not knowing the term at all
Describing it as simply 'being nice to customers' with no depth
No connection made to staff wellbeing or burnout
followUps: What could a manager actually do, day to day, to support staff dealing with this?

question: Some hospitality theorists argue that employee satisfaction is the real starting point for profitability, ahead of pricing or marketing. Do you find that argument convincing?
lookingFor: Ability to reason through a causal chain, employee satisfaction to service quality to guest loyalty to profit, with critical awareness of its limits.

bullets: Explain the underlying logic, satisfied staff deliver better service, which drives guest satisfaction and repeat business, which drives profit
Give it credit while noting it isn't the whole picture, a well-run business still needs sound pricing, location, and marketing
Reach a reasoned personal judgment rather than accepting or rejecting it outright
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I find the underlying logic genuinely convincing, in a service business the product basically is the interaction, so a resentful or exhausted employee is going to deliver worse service almost no matter how good the training or systems are, and guests notice that, which affects whether they come back. What I wouldn't accept is that it's the only lever, a beautifully run team can't rescue a badly located property or a fundamentally mispriced product, so I think of it as necessary rather than sufficient. Where I think it's most useful as an idea is as a corrective, a lot of hospitality businesses cut staffing and training first when costs get tight, and this argument is really a warning that doing that can quietly wreck the thing that actually drives repeat revenue. I'd take it seriously as a priority, without treating it as the single explanation for profitability.

commonMistakes: Simply agreeing or disagreeing with no reasoning through the causal chain
Not acknowledging other factors like pricing, location, or marketing matter too
Treating the question as unfamiliar with no attempt to reason it through
followUps: Can you think of a real business example where cutting staff investment seemed to backfire this way?

question: Medical tourism, traveling abroad for cheaper elective surgery, is a growing niche within the travel industry. What ethical issues does that raise for you?
lookingFor: Awareness of the real risk and equity issues in medical tourism beyond just seeing it as a convenient cost-saving trend.

bullets: Identify patient safety risk, variable regulatory standards and complications that surface after returning home
Consider the equity angle, medical tourism can drain resources or talent from serving local populations in the destination country
Show balanced judgment, recognizing legitimate reasons patients seek it while acknowledging these real risks
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The biggest concern for me is patient safety and continuity of care, surgical standards and regulation vary a lot between countries, and if a complication develops after the patient has flown home, follow-up care becomes genuinely difficult. There's also an equity question I think gets overlooked, in some destinations, private hospitals built to serve medical tourists compete for the same doctors and resources that the local public healthcare system needs, so a growing medical tourism industry can quietly worsen local access to care. At the same time, I understand why patients pursue it, when a procedure costs a fraction of the price and comes with a shorter wait, that's a real and legitimate pull, especially for people without good insurance. I think the honest position is that it can be done responsibly with proper accreditation and coordination with home country doctors, but the industry has real risks that get glossed over in a lot of the marketing.

commonMistakes: Only seeing medical tourism as a cost-saving convenience with no risk
Not considering the impact on the destination country's own healthcare access
No mention of continuity of care after the patient returns home
followUps: Should tourism agencies marketing medical trips have any responsibility for the medical outcomes?

question: Ski resorts and beach destinations are increasingly affected by climate change, shorter snow seasons, coral bleaching, coastal erosion. How do you think destinations should be responding?
lookingFor: Concrete awareness of a real climate impact on tourism with reasoned suggestions, not vague concern.

bullets: Name a specific, real example of climate impact on a tourism-dependent destination
Distinguish adaptation strategies from purely denying or ignoring the trend
Show awareness that diversification, not just fighting the climate trend directly, is often the realistic response
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Ski resorts in the Alps have been investing heavily in snowmaking and pushing operations to higher altitudes just to keep seasons viable, but I think that's a limited fix, it buys time rather than solving the underlying problem, and it's expensive and water intensive. What I find more interesting is destinations that are actively diversifying rather than just defending the old product, some ski towns are building out summer hiking and mountain biking tourism so they're not entirely dependent on snow reliability anymore. For coastal destinations facing coral bleaching or erosion, I think the honest answer is that some attractions simply won't be sustainable as they were, and destinations need to be planning their next identity now rather than waiting for the decline to force the issue. I think the resorts that survive well will be the ones that treat this as a strategic planning problem now, not an emergency to react to later.

commonMistakes: Vague concern about climate change with no specific tourism example
Only mentioning technical fixes like snowmaking with no discussion of longer-term diversification
Treating this as someone else's problem rather than a live industry challenge
followUps: Do you think tourists themselves are changing their travel choices because of climate concerns?

question: You're a hotel general manager facing a sharp, sudden drop in bookings. Head office wants a fifteen percent staff cost reduction within a month. How would you approach that decision?
lookingFor: Structured, humane reasoning that explores alternatives before layoffs and considers how any cuts are made and communicated.

bullets: Consider alternatives to layoffs first, reduced hours, voluntary leave, hiring freezes, before jumping to cuts
If cuts are unavoidable, describe fair, transparent criteria rather than arbitrary choices
Emphasize how the decision is communicated to both those affected and those who remain
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Before jumping to layoffs, I'd look at softer options first, reducing hours across the board, offering voluntary unpaid leave, freezing any open positions, because spreading the pain slightly across more people is often better than concentrating it fully onto a few who lose their jobs entirely. If those measures genuinely can't close the gap and layoffs become necessary, I'd want clear, defensible criteria, tied to role necessity and performance rather than anything arbitrary, and I'd document that reasoning so it holds up to scrutiny. I'd handle the actual conversations personally and honestly rather than delegating them or doing it by email, because people deserve to hear something like that directly and with some dignity. And I'd be just as deliberate about talking to the staff who remain, because morale and trust take a real hit after layoffs, and how leadership handles that moment shapes whether the team stays engaged or starts looking for the exit themselves.

commonMistakes: Jumping straight to layoffs without considering softer alternatives
No mention of fair, transparent selection criteria
Ignoring the impact on and communication with remaining staff
followUps: What would you do if head office rejected your softer alternatives and demanded layoffs immediately?

question: Your hotel markets itself as eco-friendly, but you discover the sustainability claims on its website are significantly overstated compared to what's actually being done. What would you do?
lookingFor: Willingness to prioritize honesty and correct the record over protecting the marketing angle, with a realistic sense of the reputational trade-off.

bullets: State clearly that the claims need correcting rather than being left as they are
Recognize the tension, admitting the gap risks short-term reputational damage, but so does being exposed later
Propose a constructive path, correcting the marketing honestly while genuinely closing the gap in practice
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd raise it internally straight away and push to correct the marketing, because overstated sustainability claims aren't a minor exaggeration, they're actively misleading guests who are choosing us partly for that reason, and greenwashing claims that get exposed publicly tend to do far more damage than a quieter, honest correction now. I know there's a real short-term risk in admitting the gap, it might look bad, but I think it looks a lot worse if a journalist or guest discovers the discrepancy themselves later and it becomes a bigger story. My approach would be to correct the public claims to something accurate immediately, and separately push for an actual plan with a realistic timeline to close the gap between what we say and what we do, rather than either quietly softening the claims and hoping no one notices, or leaving them as they are.

commonMistakes: Deciding to quietly leave the misleading claims as they are
Only focusing on the reputational risk of correcting it, ignoring the guest deception angle
No concrete plan to actually close the gap, just a promise to 'fix the wording'
followUps: What would you do if management resisted correcting the claims because of the marketing value they bring?

subtopic: Automation and the future of hospitality jobs
question: Some hotels have experimented with robot staff for check-in or room service delivery. Do you think automation like this is the future of the industry, or a passing novelty?
lookingFor: Grounded reasoning about which tasks automation genuinely suits versus which depend on human judgment or warmth, rather than a sweeping prediction either way.

bullets: Distinguish routine, transactional tasks that automation handles well from judgment-heavy or emotionally significant guest moments
Reference a real or plausible example rather than speaking only in the abstract
Give a reasoned prediction about where the balance likely settles rather than an all-or-nothing claim
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think automation genuinely makes sense for routine, low-judgment tasks, mobile check-in or a delivery robot bringing towels up doesn't need a human touch, and it frees staff time for interactions that actually matter more. Where I'm skeptical is the idea of automating away the moments that define good hospitality, resolving a genuine complaint, noticing a guest is having a hard trip, those need judgment and warmth that current technology doesn't really replicate convincingly. I remember reading about a hotel in Japan that experimented heavily with robot staff and ended up scaling a lot of it back because guests found it impersonal for exactly those higher-touch moments. My prediction is automation keeps expanding for logistics and routine service, but the human role shifts toward the harder, more relational parts of the job rather than disappearing.

commonMistakes: A sweeping claim that robots will either replace all hospitality staff or never matter at all
No real or plausible example given
Not distinguishing which specific tasks suit automation and which don't
followUps: What's one hospitality task you think will never be fully automated, and why?

subtopic: Space tourism as an emerging niche
question: Commercial space tourism is starting to become a real, if tiny, part of the travel industry. Do you see this as relevant to hospitality and tourism management, or is it a separate world?
lookingFor: Ability to connect an unfamiliar emerging niche back to core hospitality and tourism principles, showing flexible subject thinking.

bullets: Acknowledge the scale is currently tiny and extremely high cost, not mainstream tourism yet
Connect it back to familiar hospitality and tourism principles, guest experience design, safety, exclusivity marketing
Offer a reasoned view on whether or how it might matter to the field going forward
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It's an incredibly small, ultra-luxury niche right now, a handful of paying passengers a year, so it's nowhere near mainstream tourism. But I think it's relevant to the field precisely because the same principles apply even at that scale, someone still has to design the pre-flight experience, manage extreme guest safety and liability, and build the exclusivity and story around the trip the way luxury travel already does. It reminds me of how early commercial aviation or the first luxury cruise lines must have looked, a tiny, risky niche that gradually professionalized into a real industry segment. I'd treat it less as a separate world and more as an extreme edge case of destination and experience design, one that's worth watching because the companies behind it are already hiring hospitality-trained people to build that guest experience.

commonMistakes: Dismissing it as entirely irrelevant to hospitality with no reasoning
Overstating its current scale or mainstream relevance
Failing to connect it back to core hospitality or tourism concepts
followUps: What hospitality skill do you think would transfer most directly to that kind of extreme, high-risk guest experience?

question: As an assistant manager, you discover the property has been quietly ignoring a fire safety code violation flagged in a previous inspection, and it hasn't been fixed because of the cost. What would you do?
lookingFor: Willingness to prioritize guest and staff safety over loyalty to management or fear of conflict, with a sensible escalation approach.

bullets: State clearly that guest and staff safety takes priority over cost or internal awkwardness
Describe a sensible escalation path, raising it directly with management first before going further
Acknowledge willingness to escalate externally, to a regulator or above the immediate manager, if internal escalation is ignored
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: This isn't something I'd stay quiet about, a known fire safety violation left unfixed because of cost is a genuine risk to guests and staff, and no amount of loyalty to management justifies leaving it in place. My first step would be raising it directly and clearly with my manager or the general manager, in writing, so there's a record, and asking for a concrete timeline to fix it rather than a vague promise. If it kept being ignored or delayed without good reason, I'd escalate further, to head office or ultimately to the relevant fire safety authority, even knowing that could create real conflict at work. I'd rather deal with an uncomfortable professional relationship than the possibility of someone getting hurt in a fire that a known, fixable problem contributed to.

commonMistakes: Deciding to stay quiet to avoid conflict or protect their job
No structured escalation, jumping straight to an external report with no internal attempt first
Downplaying the seriousness of the risk
followUps: What would you do if raising it internally got you a warning to drop the issue?
